title: Matrices on the spot
objectives: Find eigenvalues of special matrices (all-ones, rank one, projections) by reasoning, not computing.

screens.title: The all-ones matrix
screens.prose: This lesson takes about 20 minutes, ninety seconds a question; say your reasoning aloud first. Find these eigenvalues without computing a determinant. Use the trace and the rank.

state.caption: The $4 \times 4$ matrix of ones: trace 4, every row the same.

screens.question: List the four eigenvalues of $J$, largest first.

hints.text: Every row is the same, so what is the rank?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the rank for how many are 0, then the trace.

byKey.r0c1: The eigenvalues add to the trace, 4. With rank 1, only one of them is non-zero.

explain.text: Every row is the same, so $J$ has rank 1 and three eigenvalues are 0. The eigenvalues add to the trace, 4, so the last one is 4. Check: $J(1, 1, 1, 1) = 4(1, 1, 1, 1)$.

screens.title: A rank-one square
screens.prose: Now $uu^\top$ with $u = (1, 2, 2)$. Every row is a multiple of $u$, so the rank is again 1.

state.caption: Each row is $u$ times one of its entries.

screens.question: What is the one non-zero eigenvalue of $uu^\top$?

hints.text: One non-zero eigenvalue, so it equals the trace.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the diagonal.

byKey.norm: You gave $|u| = 3$. The eigenvalue is $|u|^2$: $(uu^\top)u = u(u^\top u)$.
byKey.sum: You added the entries of $u$. Add the diagonal of $uu^\top$ instead.

explain.text: The trace is $1 + 4 + 4 = 9$, and rank 1 puts it all on one eigenvalue. Check: $(uu^\top)u = u\,|u|^2 = 9u$. The other two eigenvalues are 0.

screens.title: Two different vectors
screens.prose: Now $uv^\top$ with $u = (1, 2)$ and $v = (3, 4)$. It is not symmetric, but it still has rank 1.
screens.question: What is its non-zero eigenvalue?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the diagonal.

byKey.uu: You gave $|u|^2$. With two vectors the eigenvalue is $v \cdot u$.
byKey.vv: You gave $|v|^2$. The eigenvalue is $v \cdot u$.
byKey.det: The determinant is 0, so one eigenvalue is 0. The other is the trace.

explain.text: The trace is $3 + 8 = 11 = v \cdot u$, and the other eigenvalue is 0. Check: $(uv^\top)u = u\,(v \cdot u) = 11u$.

screens.title: One correlation for all
screens.prose: Five assets with pairwise correlation 0.3. The matrix is $0.7I + 0.3J$, and $J$ has eigenvalues 5, 0, 0, 0, 0.
screens.question: Fill in the eigenvalues of $R$.

hints.text: Adding $0.7I$ adds 0.7 to every eigenvalue of $0.3J$.

feedback.correct: 2.2 once, 0.7 four times; the squares add to 6.8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift the eigenvalues of $0.3J$ by 0.7.

byKey.r2c1: For a symmetric matrix this equals the sum of squared entries: $5 + 20 \times 0.09$.

explain.text: The eigenvalues are $1 + 4 \times 0.3 = 2.2$ once and $1 - 0.3 = 0.7$ four times. Check: $2.2^2 + 4 \times 0.7^2 = 6.8$, and the squared entries give $5 + 20 \times 0.09 = 6.8$.

screens.title: A reflection
screens.prose: The matrix $H = I - 2ww^\top/|w|^2$ with $w = (1, 2, 2)$ reflects space in the plane at right angles to $w$.
screens.question: Fill in its eigenvalues.

hints.text: What does a mirror do to a vector at right angles to it?
Vectors in the mirror plane stay put.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A mirror flips one direction and keeps the rest.

byKey.r0c1: The reflection sends $w$ to $-w$, so its eigenvalue is $-1$.

explain.text: $w$ flips, giving $-1$; the plane stays put, giving 1 twice. The trace checks it: $-1 + 1 + 1 = 1 = n - 2$. A projection would give 1 and 0 instead, with trace equal to rank.

screens.title: Ones are not the identity
screens.prose: A candidate says $I + J$ for $n = 3$ has eigenvalues 2, 2 and 2: one from $I$ plus one from $J$.

state.caption: Twos on the diagonal, ones elsewhere.

screens.question: What is the largest eigenvalue of $I + J$?

hints.text: What are the eigenvalues of $J$ for $n = 3$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the eigenvalues of $J$.

byKey.ones: You gave $J$ the eigenvalue 1, as if it were the identity. $J$ has 3, 0 and 0.
byKey.three: You gave the top eigenvalue of $J$. Adding $I$ adds 1.

explain.text: $J$ has eigenvalues 3, 0, 0, so $I + J$ has 4, 1, 1. The trace checks it: $4 + 1 + 1 = 6$. The all-ones matrix never has eigenvalue 1 unless $n = 1$.

screens.title: A quarter turn
screens.prose: The rotation by 90 degrees sends $(1, 0)$ to $(0, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$ to $(-1, 0)$. Its trace is 0 and its determinant is 1.
screens.question: What are the eigenvalues of $Q$?

options.why: Those belong to a reflection. A rotation turns every real vector, so none stays on its line.
They would multiply to 0, but the determinant is 1.
A rotation keeps lengths, but it moves every direction. Their sum would be 2, not the trace 0.

hints.text: Does any real vector stay on its own line?
The eigenvalues add to 0 and multiply to 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the trace and the determinant.

byKey.pm: You gave a reflection's eigenvalues. A rotation leaves no real direction alone.

explain.text: The eigenvalues add to the trace, 0, and multiply to the determinant, 1. So $\lambda^2 + 1 = 0$ and $\lambda = \pm i$. No real direction survives a quarter turn.

screens.title: Four shortcuts
screens.prose: Each time we used the structure before any arithmetic: $$\sum \lambda_i = \operatorname{tr} A, \qquad \prod \lambda_i = \det A, \qquad \sum \lambda_i^2 = \sum a_{ij}^2 \ \text{(symmetric)}.$$ The rank of a symmetric matrix counts its non-zero eigenvalues. Say it aloud: trace, rank, structure, squares.
screens.question: A symmetric matrix has rows $(2, 1)$ and $(1, 2)$, and one eigenvalue is 3. What is the other?

hints.text: The eigenvalues add to the trace, 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract 3 from the trace.

byKey.three: The trace is 4, so the two cannot both be 3.
byKey.neg: The trace is 4, so the other is $4 - 3 = 1$.

explain.text: The trace is 4, so the other eigenvalue is $4 - 3 = 1$. The squares check it: $9 + 1 = 10 = 4 + 1 + 1 + 4$.

screens.title: Why rank one is easy
screens.prose: Put the argument in order. One line does not belong.
screens.question: Order the steps that find the eigenvalues of $uv^\top$.

lines.text: For any square matrix, the eigenvalues add to the trace.
$uv^\top$ sends every vector to a multiple of $u$, so it has rank 1.
Its null space has dimension $n - 1$, so $n - 1$ eigenvalues are 0.
So the remaining eigenvalue equals the trace.
The trace of $uv^\top$ is $\sum u_i v_i = v \cdot u$, and indeed $(uv^\top)u = (v \cdot u)\,u$.
A rank-one matrix has one direction, so its eigenvalue is 1.
lines.why: That confuses the number of directions with the size of the stretch. The stretch along $u$ is $v \cdot u$.

hints.text: The trace gives the last one.

feedback.correct: Trace, rank, zeros, then the last eigenvalue.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the zeros first, then use the trace.

byKey.d1: One direction does not mean a stretch of 1. The stretch is $v \cdot u$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line that belongs. Only one line is wrong.

explain.text: Rank 1 forces $n - 1$ zero eigenvalues. The trace then hands the last one over: $v \cdot u$. The all-ones matrix is the case $u = v = (1, \ldots, 1)$, giving $n$.

screens.title: The market factor
screens.prose: Five assets with pairwise correlation 0.3, as before. The top eigenvector $(1, 1, 1, 1, 1)$ is the "market": every asset moving together. The eigenvalues add to the trace, 5.
screens.question: What share of the total variance does the market component carry?

hints.text: Share is the eigenvalue over the trace.

byKey.rho: You gave the correlation. The share is the top eigenvalue over the trace.
byKey.raw: You typed the top eigenvalue, 2.2. Divide it by the trace: $2.2/5 = 0.44$, which is 44%.
byKey.frac: You typed the fraction 0.44 in a per cent box. Type 44 instead.

explain.text: $2.2/5 = 44\%$ of the variance sits in the market component. Each other component carries $0.7/5 = 14\%$. Higher correlation pushes more into the market.

screens.title: The follow-up: and the determinant
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: and the determinant of that $5 \times 5$ matrix?
screens.question: What is $\det R$?

hints.text: The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply all five eigenvalues.

byKey.once: You used 0.7 once. It appears four times: $2.2 \times 0.7^4$.
byKey.sum: You added the eigenvalues, which gives the trace. Multiply them.

explain.text: $\det R = 2.2 \times 0.7^4 = 2.2 \times 0.2401 = 0.52822$. As the correlation rises, the four small eigenvalues shrink and the determinant falls towards 0.

ideas: The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues and the determinant their product.
A rank-one matrix $uv^\top$ has one non-zero eigenvalue, $v \cdot u$; the all-ones matrix has $n$.
Equicorrelation gives $1 + (n - 1)\rho$ once and $1 - \rho$ for the rest.

formula.name: Shortcuts
formula.note: For a symmetric matrix, the squares of the eigenvalues add to the squares of the entries.

summary.trap: The all-ones matrix has eigenvalues $n$ and 0, never 1.

quiz.question: What is the largest eigenvalue of the $5 \times 5$ matrix of ones?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rank 1, so the eigenvalue is the trace.

byKey.one: The all-ones matrix is not the identity. Its top eigenvalue is $n$.
byKey.all: You added every entry. Add the diagonal.

explain.text: Rank 1 and trace 5, so the eigenvalues are 5, 0, 0, 0, 0.

quiz.question: What is the non-zero eigenvalue of $uu^\top$ for $u = (3, 4)$?

byKey.sum: You added the entries of $u$. Add their squares.

quiz.question: A projection in five dimensions maps onto a plane. What is its trace?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Its eigenvalues are 1 on the plane and 0 off it.

byKey.five: You counted every dimension. Directions off the plane give 0.
byKey.one: A plane has two directions, each with eigenvalue 1.

explain.text: Eigenvalues 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, so the trace is 2. For a projection the trace equals the rank.

quiz.question: Three assets with pairwise correlation 0.5. What is the smallest eigenvalue of their correlation matrix?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The small eigenvalues are $1 - \rho$.

byKey.zero: Only a perfect correlation drives them to 0.

explain.text: The eigenvalues are $1 + 2 \times 0.5 = 2$ once and $1 - 0.5 = 0.5$ twice.
